Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I put on loud music or TV
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
People are not what they seem
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette: Elena, an American citizen of Latin American descent, carried the night she crossed the border like a stone in her chest. The memory did not fade; it arrived with the stark clarity of a photograph. She remembered the damp air, the weight of her family's belongings, and the sudden flare of a flashlight cutting through the trees. When they were stopped at a checkpoint, men in dark uniforms emerged from the shadows. Their boots struck the pavement in rhythm. Someone shouted a command in Spanish, loud and immediate. The air hung thick with the sharp, chemical bite of poured alcohol from a canteen someone had taken from the vehicle behind them. Elena had come to believe that survival depended on reading the exact tilt of a man's shoulders, on obeying without hesitation. Sometimes, hours later, the sound of a raised voice would pull the checkpoint back into focus, and she would hear the exact cadence of the officers' commands echoing in her mind. When the memory returned, the flood of emotion was so sudden and heavy that she would have to stop whatever she was doing, press her palms against her thighs, and wait for the wave to pass. In the months that followed, her daily life became a series of careful calculations. She found herself avoiding parking structures where security guards patrolled in crisp uniforms. The sight of anyone in uniform made her breath catch. When a supervisor at a previous job raised his voice to give directions, her shoulders would lock, and she would step aside, waiting for the instruction to pass. She began to map her environment with precise attention, always choosing seats with a solid wall at her back and a clear line to the door. She told herself it was simply practical, but what frightened her most was how quickly her pulse would climb when a chair scraped against the floor or a colleague walked up behind her unexpectedly. Her mind, she noticed, had become a watchtower. She reacted to the echo of a dropped book as if a warning had just been sounded. At the same time, she spent hours replaying the night of the crossing, turning over every possible decision, certain that if only she had spoken faster, moved sooner, or chosen a different route, the fear would not have been so absolute. She needed the television running at full volume before she could sleep, the noise filling the spaces where silence would let the past return. Her role as a prison guard forced her to navigate a world that mirrored the past, even as she stood on the other side of the fence. She could not change the architecture of the yard or the standard-issue fatigues worn by the entire staff. During her morning briefing, when the warden paced the room and barked out daily assignments, Elena would feel a familiar tightening in her chest. She had started sitting in the last row, far from the podium, convincing herself it was because she wanted to take better notes. Her husband, Mateo, noticed how she flinched when the door to their apartment closed too quickly, how she kept her answers measured when new neighbors arrived or coworkers offered casual suggestions. She felt like a stranger to herself, as if the person who could walk through a checkpoint without breaking had disappeared entirely. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place and that trust was a vulnerability. The work of maintaining this vigilance was exhausting. Last week, during a lockdown drill, a sudden alarm blared and a fellow officer ran past her station. Elena's body moved before her mind could catch up, her hand instinctively dropping to her empty belt loop as her breath came in short, sharp gasps. Mateo found her afterward sitting in the patrol car, staring at her hands, unable to explain why her body still treated the present as a threat. She had come to therapy because the exhaustion was no longer just physical; it was a quiet erosion of the life she had built. She was terrified that she would never stop waiting for the next command, that the world would remain a place where uniformed figures and the smell of spilled liquor could still pull her back into the dark. What she hoped for, though she struggled to name it aloud, was simply to sit in a room without checking the exits, to hear a voice without bracing, and to recognize herself again.
